config.title: Rate limiting & security headers

intro.title: Rate limiting & security headers
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a secure Express.js server that protects against excessive requests and common web vulnerabilities. You will learn to implement rate limiting to control how many requests a client can make in a given time period, preventing abuse. Additionally, you will set security headers to defend against attacks like cross-site scripting (XSS) and clickjacking. The main technologies used are the Express framework, the `express-rate-limit` middleware for rate limiting, and the `helmet` middleware for security headers. By the end, you'll have a server that is more resilient and safer for real-world use.
intro.usecase: Rate limiting and security headers are essential for protecting production APIs from abuse and attacks. You'll implement these in Express when building public-facing endpoints like user registration forms, payment processing APIs, or dashboard data feeds. For example, an e-commerce site uses rate limiting to prevent bots from brute-forcing login attempts, while security headers like Content-Security-Policy protect customer dashboards from XSS attacks. As a developer, you'll configure these safeguards to ensure your applications remain available and secure under real traffic conditions.

objectives: Configure an Express application to apply rate limiting to incoming requests.
Integrate a middleware to set essential security headers in an Express server.
Construct a custom rate limiter with configurable window and maximum request limits.
Apply security headers to mitigate common web vulnerabilities like XSS and clickjacking.
Manipulate response headers to enforce content security policies and control MIME types.
Initialize and bind a rate limiting middleware to specific routes or the entire application.
Update an existing Express server to include both rate limiting and security header protections.

steps.title: Import Express and required middleware packages
steps.instruction: Import Express, express-rate-limit, and helmet using require statements at the top of your file.
steps.hint: Use the require() function to import each package. Remember to assign them to variables with appropriate names.
steps.seedCode:
// Import Express, express-rate-limit, and helmet here

// Your Express app will be created in the next steps
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have three require statements that import the necessary packages for rate limiting and security headers.
successCriteria: Express, express-rate-limit, and helmet are imported using require statements with appropriate variable names.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've imported some packages, but make sure you have all three: Express, express-rate-limit, and helmet. Check your require statements.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are missing or incorrect. You need to use require() to import Express, express-rate-limit, and helmet packages.

steps.title: Initialize the Express application
steps.instruction: Create an Express app instance by calling express() and assign it to a constant named 'app'.
steps.hint: Use the imported express function to create your application instance.
steps.analogousExample:
// Creating an Express app instance
const app = express();
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a constant named 'app' that holds your Express application instance, ready for middleware configuration.
successCriteria: The Express app instance is created and assigned to a constant named 'app'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling express() to create the instance and assigning it to a constant named 'app'.
steps.feedbackWrong: create the Express app instance by calling the imported express function and assigning it to a constant named 'app'.

steps.title: Configure rate limiting middleware
steps.instruction: Create a rate limiter instance using express-rate-limit with a window of 15 minutes and a maximum of 100 requests per window.
steps.hint: Use the rateLimit function imported from 'express-rate-limit' to create a middleware instance with configuration options.
steps.expectedOutcome: A rate limiter instance is created with proper configuration for windowMs and max requests.
successCriteria: The rate limiter instance is created with windowMs set to 15 minutes (900000 ms) and max set to 100 requests.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a rate limiter, but check the configuration values. The window should be 15 minutes (15 * 60 * 1000 ms) and max should be 100 requests.
steps.feedbackWrong: The rate limiter instance wasn't created correctly. Make sure to use the rateLimit function with the proper configuration object.

steps.title: Apply rate limiting to all routes
steps.instruction: Use app.use() to apply the rate limiter middleware to your entire Express application.
steps.hint: Call app.use() and pass your rate limiter instance as the argument. This will make the rate limiting apply to all incoming requests.
steps.expectedOutcome: The rate limiter middleware is now applied globally to protect all endpoints in your application.
successCriteria: app.use() is called with the rate limiter instance as its argument
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling app.use() with the rate limiter instance as the argument.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try using app.use() to apply the rate limiter middleware to your entire application.

steps.title: Configure Helmet security headers
steps.instruction: Initialize the Helmet middleware with default security headers by calling helmet() and storing it in a variable named helmetMiddleware.
steps.hint: Remember that helmet() returns a middleware function. Assign the result to a const variable.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: initializing middleware
const helmetMiddleware = helmet();
steps.expectedOutcome: The Helmet middleware is initialized and ready to be applied to the Express app.
successCriteria: A variable named helmetMiddleware is declared and assigned the result of calling helmet().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling helmet() and storing the result in a variable named helmetMiddleware.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Helmet middleware wasn't initialized correctly. Check that you're calling helmet() and assigning it to helmetMiddleware.

steps.title: Apply Helmet middleware
steps.instruction: Apply the Helmet middleware globally to your Express app using app.use().
steps.hint: Use app.use() with the helmet() function as the argument.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Helmet middleware is applied globally to add security headers to all responses.
successCriteria: Helmet middleware is applied using app.use(helmet()).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using app.use() with helmet() as the argument.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the syntax for applying middleware. Use app.use(helmet()) to apply Helmet globally.

steps.title: Create a test route to verify rate limiting
steps.instruction: Add a GET route at path '/' that returns a JSON response with a message property set to 'Hello, rate-limited world!'.
steps.hint: Use app.get() to define the route. The callback should send a JSON response using res.json().
steps.expectedOutcome: A GET route is defined at the root path that returns a JSON message, which will be used to test rate limiting.
successCriteria: The route is defined with app.get('/', ...) and returns a JSON object with a message property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using app.get() with the correct path and returning JSON with a message.
steps.feedbackWrong: The route isn't defined correctly. Check the path and response format.

steps.title: Add error handling for rate limit exceeded
steps.instruction: Add a custom error handler for when the rate limit is exceeded by setting the `handler` option in your rate limiter configuration.
steps.hint: The rate limiter instance accepts a `handler` function that receives the request, response, and next parameters. Use it to send a custom JSON error message.
steps.expectedOutcome: The rate limiter will now respond with a custom JSON error message when the limit is exceeded.
successCriteria: The rate limiter configuration includes a `handler` function that sends a JSON response with status 429.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the handler might be missing the status code or JSON response. Ensure it sends a 429 status with a JSON error message.
steps.feedbackWrong: The rate limiter configuration doesn't include a custom error handler. Add a `handler` function to the limiter configuration that responds with a 429 status and JSON error.

steps.title: Configure custom security headers
steps.instruction: Add custom middleware after the Helmet middleware to set specific security headers like X-Content-Type-Options and X-Frame-Options.
steps.hint: Use app.use() with a function that sets headers on the response object.
steps.expectedOutcome: The application now includes custom middleware that sets additional security headers on all responses.
successCriteria: Custom middleware is added after Helmet and sets at least X-Content-Type-Options and X-Frame-Options headers.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added middleware, but make sure it sets both X-Content-Type-Options and X-Frame-Options headers and is placed after the Helmet middleware.
steps.feedbackWrong: The custom security headers middleware is missing or incomplete. Add middleware that sets X-Content-Type-Options and X-Frame-Options headers.

steps.title: Start the Express server
steps.instruction: Start the Express server by calling app.listen() on port 3000 and add a console log message that says 'Server running on port 3000'.
steps.hint: Use app.listen() with the port number and a callback function that logs the message to the console.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will start on port 3000 and display a confirmation message in the console.
successCriteria: The server is started with app.listen() on port 3000 and logs 'Server running on port 3000'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're calling app.listen() with port 3000 and a callback that logs the message.
steps.feedbackWrong: The server isn't starting correctly. Check that you're using app.listen() with the right port and console.log().
